item.title: A single AI model simulates the behavior of many substances, from sliding sand to folding proteins
item.description: By learning how matter moves, the WorldParticle system could assist with developing soft robots, medicines, and more.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.ns2:encoded:
Today, a scientist who wants to simulate a physical process must pick the right tool for that one job, such as a solver built for flowing water or another designed to model the way a protein folds. Each one is hand-coded around the specific equations that dictate how that process behaves.

Researchers at MIT, the University of British Columbia (UBC), and elsewhere have now replaced that pa
item.ns3:content: “It is a similar architecture to ChatGPT. But instead of predicting one word at a time to write a piece of text, we are predicting how these particles will move, one step at a time,” says Peter Yichen Chen. Credit: Courtesy of the researchers
item.category: Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL)

item.title: AI-assisted learning platform helps robots reason beyond literal commands
item.description: The new approach, known as FLEX, could lead to more intuitive, interactive household and assistive robots.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Chu | MIT News
item.ns2:encoded:
Humans are intuitive by nature. We can sense meaning beyond the literal words that we encounter. Now, a new artificial intelligence-assisted learning platform developed by MIT engineers is enabling robots to read larger meaning into a human’s natural language commands. 

In a study to be presented at the annual Conference on Robot Learning this month, researchers from MIT and New York
item.ns3:content: With a new system designed by researchers from MIT and New York University, humans can interact with a robot by giving it instructions in natural, conversational language. The robot can not only follow the instructions literally, but also read into the words to draw larger generalizations that help to improve its motion-planning task. Credit: Getty Images, MIT News
item.category: Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL)

item.title: How to predict the behavior of molecules from scant data
item.description: A machine-learning approach called CheMeleon provides a practical way to develop new drugs or other molecules with much less detailed, expensive experimentation.
item.dc:creator: David L. Chandler | Department of Chemical Engineering
item.ns2:encoded: Discovering new molecules for specific uses is a major driver of progress in a wide variety of industries, whether it’s pharmaceutical companies looking for new drugs, or electronics or energy companies seeking new materials with particular properties. But it’s also largely a trial-and-error process, because there is not yet any way to perfectly predict how a given chemical compound will behave
item.ns3:content: Like a chameleon changing colors, CheMeleon adapts a single pre-trained model to predict many different molecular properties, such as potency (pEC50), toxicity (LD50), and solubility (logS). The MIT-developed model first learns chemistry by predicting easy-to-compute molecular descriptors for about a million molecules, then fine-tunes to each new task. Image courtesy o

item.title: Clearing up a robot’s fuzzy memory
item.description: A new system identifies and corrects unreliable object descriptions stored in a robot’s memory, improving the robot’s ability to interact with its environment.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.ns2:encoded:
In an emergency, a human might someday ask a robotic assistant to fetch a wall-mounted defibrillator located down the hall. But if the robot has incorrectly labeled the defibrillator as a fire extinguisher in its stored memory, it may not know where to find the life-saving device.

This robotic assistant could benefit from a new memory system created by MIT researchers. The system identifi
item.ns3:content: “Allowing a robot to know what it doesn’t know is going to be essential for this technology to be deployed safely and have a positive impact on society,” says Luca Carlone. Credit: MIT News; Getty Images
item.category: Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS)

item.title: Building connections across the research infrastructure
item.description: MIT.nano and the Northeast Microelectronics Coalition gathered facility leaders and technology professionals from across the nation to explore ways to make shared-access facilities more connected.
item.dc:creator: MIT.nano
item.ns2:encoded: Running a modern research laboratory requires more than maintaining sophisticated instruments. Researchers need to complete training, obtain access, schedule and operate equipment, navigate billing, and more. For large, shared facilities, coordinating these activities across hundreds of instruments and thousands of users can be a significant undertaking. As research becomes increasingly interdi
item.ns3:content: The 2026 NEMO user meeting, hosted by MIT.nano and sponsored by the Northeast Microelectronics Coalition (NEMC) hub, brought together representatives from 25 laboratories and organizations across the nation to explore ways to make shared-access facilities more connected. Photo: Dave Terry/MIT.nano

item.title: Powering up for a pivotal moment
item.description: From a nuclear revival to qubits, the MIT Energy Initiative’s annual research conference tracked deployment of today’s technologies to discovery of tomorrow’s breakthroughs.
item.dc:creator: Leda Zimmerman | MIT Energy Initiative
item.ns2:encoded:
Utilizing waste carbon at scale, assessing public trust in artificial intelligence and data centers, and building a quantum toolkit for critical applications were among the topics energy experts explored at the MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI)’s annual research conference on Sept. 22-23.

The complexity of the energy transition demands “a truly interdisciplinary and international approach,” s
item.ns3:content: At the 2026 Energizing@MIT: MITEI’s Annual Research Conference, MITEI principal research scientist Deepjyoti Deka (left) presented his Seed Innovation Fund project on accelerating energy planning in the era of data centers through generative AI. Photo: Jake Belcher

item.title: Regina Barzilay and Jim Collins win Pritzker Prize for AI and Science Research Excellence for work in AI-enabled antibiotic discovery
item.description: The MIT professors collaborated to identify the first AI-discovered antibiotic, a scientific breakthrough that is widely recognized as a milestone in AI-driven drug discovery.
item.dc:creator: Alex Ouyang | Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health
item.ns2:encoded: Regina Barzilay, MIT’s School of Engineering Distinguished Professor of AI and Health, and James Collins, MIT’s Termeer Professor of Medical Engineering and Science, are the recipients of the 2026 Pritzker Prize for AI in Scie
item.ns3:content: Regina Barzilay (left) and James Collins are the recipients of this year’s 2026 Pritzker Prize for AI in Science Research Excellence, which is jointly awarded by the University of Chicago and Caltech. Photos: Max Rousseau (Barzilay) and M. Scott Brauer (Collins)

Five MIT faculty members and two additional alumni were recently named to the 2026 cohort of AI2050 Fellows. The honor is announced annually by Schmidt Sciences, Eric and Wendy Schmidt’s philanthropic initiative that aims to accelerate scientific innovation.

item.title: Q&A: Hey AI, who should I vote for this year?
item.description: MIT professors Adam Berinsky and Chara Podimata discuss a new project to track how AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Abby Abazorius | MIT News
item.ns2:encoded:
People are peppering artificial intelligence chatbots everyday with questions, but when it comes to politics and the looming 2026 U.S. midterm elections, what role are AI platforms playing? Could an AI chatbot sway a voter to switch parties or re-examine their political beliefs? 

MIT researchers have built a new dashboard, called the
item.ns3:content: The LLM Election Observatory is a dashboard built by MIT researchers that examines, in real-time, how popular AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 midterm elections. Credit: MIT News
item.category: Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS)
School of Humanities Arts and Social Sciences

item.title: 3 Questions: Why infrastructure is entering a defining era
item.description: Professor Ali Jadbabaie describes how AI, digital transformation, climate change, and complex geopolitics are forcing engineers and policymakers to rethink how infrastructure is designed, built, and managed.
item.dc:creator: Stephanie Martinovich | Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering
item.ns2:encoded:
For centuries, infrastructure has evolved alongside technology. New materials and engineering techniques enabled taller buildings, longer bridges, and larger cities. Computing and digital technologies later transformed how infrastructure was designed, monitored, and operated.

Now, the pace of change is accelerating, and challenges are arriving simultaneously. Climate change i
item.ns3:content: “Designing infrastructure is a highly transdisciplinary, sociotechnical endeavor, involving social, technical, and economic considerations. Understanding how these systems are designed is increasingly important because they are becoming more complex, making decision-making particularly difficult,” says Ali Jadbabaie, JR East Professor and head of the Department of Civil and Environm

item.title: Making machines that can listen
item.description: Professor Paris Smaragdis develops computers with superhuman hearing for applications like speech recognition, music understanding, and environmental monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.ns2:encoded:
The crack of a bat accompanied by a roar from the crowd can capture a baseball fan’s attention, even if they miss seeing the home run. Humans may be visual creatures, but we also perceive the world around us by listening to it. 

To improve artificial perception, MIT Professor Paris Smaragdis SM ’97, PhD ’01 seeks to make machines that can hear and understand sound even better than hu
item.ns3:content: To improve artificial perception, Professor Paris Smaragdis seeks to make machines that can hear and understand sound even better than humans. Image: Jake Belcher
item.category: School of Humanities Arts and Social Sciences

item.title: Learner collaborates with MIT peers to develop book of AI insights
item.description: Prabha Jha used her experience with MIT Open Learning’s program for senior executives to develop AI solutions for her employer, Verizon, and to write a book.
item.dc:creator: Caroline Maselli | MIT Open Learning
item.ns2:encoded:
Like many leaders today, Prabha Jha has been feeling the significant impact artificial intelligence is having on business operations. While the rapid evolution of the technology can bring fear, uncertainty, and confusion, Jha chose a different response: excitement. She began asking herself, “How do I become part of this once-in-a-lifetime thing?” 

Jha holds a bach
item.ns3:content: Through her experiences with an AI for Senior Executives course from MIT Open Learning, Prabha Jha and 20 peer leaders released “The AI Anthology,” a collection of essays examining the influence AI has had across industries and across society. Photo courtesy of the subject.

item.title: At New York Climate Week 2026, MIT connects with a global network
item.description: A cross-section of the MIT community convened discussions on topics ranging from data centers and super pollutants to agriculture and education.
item.dc:creator: Marika McCoola | Office of the Vice President for Energy and Climate
item.ns2:encoded:
Each year, Climate Week NYC brings together more than 100,000 people in more than 1,000 events across the city to discuss climate challenges, explore solutions, and spur action. Participants come from industry, academia, philanthropy, nonprofits, government, and finance and venture capital. And this year, the mix included a strong, cross-campus presence from MIT.

item.ns3:content: Aaron Krol, managing editor of the MIT Climate Change Engagement Program, led MIT’s Climate Week NYC session “Climate Communication for Impact,” which featured (left to right) Allison Crimmins of Talking Climate, Arielle Tannenbaum of Climate Central, and Mallika Talwar of Yale University. Photo: Justin Coleman

item.title: At MIT, Martha Minow speaks on sustaining democracy, both by using and overcoming AI
item.description: In Compton Lecture, the distinguished legal scholar warns of potential “loss of the Enlightenment” while suggesting ways innovations can meet our civic and cultural needs.
item.dc:creator: Peter Dizikes | MIT News
item.ns2:encoded:
Legal scholar Martha Minow delivered this fall’s Compton Lecture at MIT on Thursday, examining the civic foundations of democracy — and describing how artificial intelligence is undermining it, but could be used to help reinforce traditional U.S. governance. 

“It’s not a good time for democracy or constitutionalism,” said Minow, who is the 300th Anniversary University Professor at Ha
item.ns3:content: Martha Minow, legal scholar and 300th Anniversary University Professor at Harvard University, delivering the Karl Taylor Compton Lecture at MIT. Photo: Jake Belcher

item.title: Reinforcing the value of human understanding at MIT
item.description: During the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences’ 75th Anniversary Symposium, President Sally Kornbluth said “MIT has never needed your particular insight and guidance more than we do now.”
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Daniel | School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences
item.ns2:encoded:
At the MIT School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) 75th Anniversary Symposium, speakers celebrated the school’s value and contributions, while exploring how artificial intelligence is transforming many aspects of teaching, research, and society.

The symposium was held Sept. 24-25 in the Linde Music Building’s Thomas Tull Concert Hall. Scholars, students
item.ns3:content: The Teaching and Learning Innovations panel at SHASS’ 75th Anniversary Symposium featured (left to right) professors Eric Klopfer, Norvin Richards, and Stephanie Seed; Senior Lecturer Sara Ellison; Institute Professor Suzanne Berger; Senior Lecturer Takako Aikawa; and Professor Will Broadhead. item.description: Assistant Professor Benjamin Lindquist studies how engineers deliberately injected randomness into early AI, giving rise to deep-learning models that sometimes hallucinate.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.ns2:encoded: Generative artificial intelligence models are rooted in ideas of mid-20th century engineers who thought some amount of irrationality was essential for a machine that could think like a human, contends Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in the MIT History Section, who holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Comput
item.ns3:content: MIT Assistant Professor Benjamin Lindquist discusses his research on the incorporation of randomness and irrationality into early AI models designed to mimic human creativity. Credit: Jared Charney

item.title: This design software reimagines everyday objects as self-aware devices
item.description: “X-Hinges” helps design and 3D print items like lamps and gloves with an interactive twist: automatically embedded sensors that perceive and adaptively respond to human contact.
item.dc:creator: Alex Shipps | MIT CSAIL
item.ns2:encoded: As a child, you likely saw a few Disney movies depicting inanimate objects, such as clocks, cups, and toys, as interactive companions to humans — an act of pure magic, seemingly. But scientists at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) are now doing something similar: transforming sta
item.ns3:content: “It’s kind of like adding a conscious element to everyday objects,” says Jiaji Li, MIT postdoc and CSAIL researcher. “In the same way an AI agent is programmed to make certain decisions based on our instructions, these creations have built-in sensing to adaptively react to human touch.” Image courtesy of the researchers.
item.category: Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL)

item.title: Why teaching AI about symmetry could make prenatal diagnosis more reliable
item.description: A model developed by researchers at MIT and Boston Children's Hospital adjusts scans on the fly to track fetal movement, potentially sparing families repeat hospital visits.
item.dc:creator: Alex Ouyang | Abdul Latif Jameel Clinic for Machine Learning in Health
item.ns2:encoded:
Despite millions of years of evolution, the development of the human fetus remains a complex process that is vulnerable to genetic, environmental, and metabolic disruptions. These disruptions could result in developmental abnormalities, starting with one of the first organs to begin developing in the fetus that continues to develop after birth: the brain.

In a routine
item.ns3:content: An MRI scan of a fetal brain (outlined in yellow) in the sagittal position. E(3)-Pose is a model that helps track movement in an MRI of the fetus’s brain. The model could help clinicians make earlier and more accurate diagnoses of developmental anomalies. Image courtesy of the MIT Jameel Clinic and the researchers.
item.category: Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL)

item.title: Giving AI a “crystal clear” view of the materials world
item.description: New research can help AI models understand crystalline materials in 3D and reason about their properties.
item.dc:creator: Zach Winn | MIT News
item.ns2:encoded:
In principle, artificial intelligence could make finding the right material for an application as simple as ordering dinner: Scientists would tell a large language model what they want, and it would serve them the perfect material for the job.

item.ns3:content: MIT researchers created an AI model that can identify optimal crystalline materials for various applications. Image: MIT News; Getty Images

Kendall Square in Cambridge, Massachusetts, is often cited as the most innovative square mile in the world. But when the Kendall Square Association gathered local stakeholders for its 18th Annual Meeting Thursday, the conversation focused on innovation primarily in the context of community.
